title: Shoftim: even the king reads (Deuteronomy 17:18–20)
hookLine: the king writes his own copy of the Torah so his heart isn't lifted up
tomorrow: Shoftim: is the tree a man? (Deuteronomy 20:19)

cards: In the ancient world, a king was the law. His word settled things. His image was on the coins.
Scribes carved his victories into stone.
The idea that a king might have to sit down with a pen and copy out somebody else's law, by hand, every word, and then read it every day of his life, would have sounded absurd in most royal courts.
Deuteronomy's chapter on kings is short, and mostly a list of limits. And it ends with an assignment.

teach.b: First the limits. If Israel sets a king over itself, he must not pile up horses, or take many wives, or heap up silver and gold. Power, pleasure, money: the three things kings usually collect.

teach.h: WRITE HIM A COPY OF THIS LAW.
teach.b: In the old Jewish translation: when he sits on his throne, "he shall write him a copy of this law in a book." And it shall be with him, "and he shall read therein all the days of his life." Why?
The verse says it plainly: "that his heart be not lifted up above his brethren." The king is still one of them.

The Talmud, in Sanhedrin, adds that the king writes a scroll of his own, kept with him wherever he goes, even into battle. And it notes that every Jew is commanded to write a Torah scroll; the king just has an extra one.
The phrase for a copy of this law is mishneh hatorah. It's where Deuteronomy gets its Greek name, second law.
Over a thousand years later, Maimonides borrowed the same words for his great law code, the Mishneh Torah.

The king reading every day is a picture of power under something bigger than itself: not the king's word over the law, but the law over the king's word. Reading isn't a reward for the powerful. It's a brake.

how: Jewish law counts writing a Torah scroll as a commandment for every Jew; many fulfill it today by sponsoring or writing a single letter in a community's new scroll, and the king's special scroll is discussed in the Talmud and Maimonides.

games.q: you've just been crowned king of Israel. what's the first thing Deuteronomy tells you to do on your throne?
o: write a copy of the law for yourself, and read it daily.
games.why: he shall write him a copy of this law in a book, and read therein all the days of his life.

practice: Think of a place where you hold some power: a parent, a manager, the one who knows most in the room, the oldest sibling.

Bring to mind a line, from scripture, a teacher or your grandmother, that puts that power back in its place, something like: you are one of them. Say it slowly, twice, and let it sit above you for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Shoftim. Judges. The portion where even the king must write the law down and read it every day.

orig.note: Hebrew: a copy, or repetition, of the law. the source of Deuteronomy's Greek name, and of Maimonides' Mishneh Torah.
